name: Density
assumptions: The sample is uniform (or ρ is an average). Volume by displacement assumes the sample does not absorb or dissolve in the water.
example: A 100.0 g iron sample displaces 12.7 mL: ρ = 100.0 g / 12.7 cm³ = 7.87 g/cm³.
mistakes: Using the total water level instead of the change in level; forgetting that 1 mL = 1 cm³.

name: Average speed
assumptions: Gives the average over the interval; the instantaneous speed may differ.
example: A cart travels 2.0 m in 1.6 s: v = 1.25 m/s.
mistakes: Confusing speed (scalar) with velocity (vector, includes direction).

name: Acceleration
assumptions: Average acceleration over the interval; constant acceleration makes it equal the instantaneous value.
example: Speed rises from 0 to 3.0 m/s in 1.5 s: a = 2.0 m/s².
mistakes: Dividing the final speed by time without subtracting the initial speed.

name: Newton's second law
assumptions: F is the net (resultant) force; valid for speeds much smaller than the speed of light.
example: A 2.0 kg cart accelerating at 1.5 m/s² needs a net force of 3.0 N.
mistakes: Using one force instead of the net force; using grams instead of kilograms.

name: Weight
assumptions: Near Earth's surface g ≈ 9.81 m/s². Weight is a force; mass is the amount of matter.
example: A 5.0 kg block weighs 5.0 × 9.81 = 49 N.
mistakes: Treating mass and weight as the same quantity.

name: Work done by a constant force
display: W = F × d (force along the displacement)
assumptions: Constant force parallel to the displacement; otherwise use W = F d cos θ.
example: Pushing with 10 N over 3.0 m does 30 J of work.
mistakes: Counting forces perpendicular to the motion, which do no work.

name: Kinetic energy
assumptions: Classical mechanics (v much less than c).
example: A 2.0 kg cart at 3.0 m/s has Eₖ = 9.0 J.
mistakes: Forgetting to square the speed; doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy.

name: Gravitational potential energy
assumptions: Uniform gravitational field near Earth's surface; uses standard g = 9.80665 m/s².
example: Lifting 2.0 kg by 1.5 m stores 29 J.
mistakes: Using it for large heights where g changes; measuring h along a slope instead of vertically.

name: Power
assumptions: Average power over the interval.
example: Transferring 600 J in 2 minutes (120 s) is 5 W.
mistakes: Mixing up energy (J) and power (J/s = W).

name: Momentum
assumptions: Momentum is a vector; direction matters when adding momenta.
example: A 0.5 kg cart at 2 m/s has p = 1 kg·m/s.
mistakes: Adding momenta of objects moving in opposite directions without signs.

name: Ohm's law
assumptions: Applies to ohmic conductors at constant temperature; filament lamps and diodes are non-ohmic.
example: 12 V across 24 Ω drives 0.5 A.
mistakes: Using the battery's EMF instead of the voltage actually across the component.

name: Electrical power
assumptions: Instantaneous power in a DC circuit.
example: A lamp with 12 V across it and 0.5 A through it uses 6 W.
mistakes: Confusing power (W) with energy (J or kWh).

name: Electrical energy
assumptions: Constant power over the time interval.
example: A 6 W lamp on for 1 hour uses 21 600 J (6 Wh).
mistakes: Forgetting to convert hours to seconds (or use Wh).

name: Electric charge
assumptions: Constant current.
example: 2.0 A for 60 s moves 120 C.
mistakes: Mixing up charge (C) and current (C/s).

name: Faraday's law of electrolysis
assumptions: All the current drives the one reaction (100 % current efficiency).
mistakes: Using z per atom instead of per molecule (H₂ needs 2 electrons).

name: Resistance of a wire
assumptions: Uniform wire at constant temperature.
example: 1 m of 1 mm² copper wire: R = 1.68×10⁻⁸ × 1 / 10⁻⁶ = 0.0168 Ω.
mistakes: Using diameter instead of cross-sectional area.

name: Ideal gas law
assumptions: Ideal gas: molecules have negligible volume and no attractions. Good at low pressure and high temperature.
example: 1.00 mol at 273.15 K and 101 325 Pa occupies 0.0224 m³ (22.4 L).
mistakes: Using °C instead of kelvin; mixing litres with m³.

name: Molar concentration
assumptions: V is the volume of solution, not of solvent (they are almost equal for dilute solutions).
example: 0.50 mol of NaCl in 2.0 L gives 0.25 mol/L.
mistakes: Using millilitres without converting to litres.

name: pH
assumptions: Uses concentration in place of activity, which is accurate only for dilute solutions. pH 7 is neutral at 25 °C only.
example: [H⁺] = 1.0×10⁻³ mol/L gives pH 3.0. A tenfold dilution of a strong acid raises pH by about 1.
mistakes: Thinking pH is linear: pH 3 is ten times more acidic than pH 4, not one 'unit' more.

name: Heat and temperature change
assumptions: No phase change occurs; c is constant over the temperature range.
example: Heating 200 g of water by 10 K needs 200 × 4.18 × 10 = 8360 J.
mistakes: Applying it during melting or boiling, when heat changes the state instead of the temperature.

name: Latent heat
assumptions: Temperature stays constant during the phase change at fixed pressure.
example: Boiling away 50 g of water needs 50 × 2257 = 112 850 J.
mistakes: Expecting the temperature to rise while water is boiling.

name: Heat loss (Newton's law of cooling)
assumptions: UA combines conduction, convection and radiation; it is roughly constant only for modest temperature differences.
example: An insulated heater with UA = 0.5 W/K at 60 K above room loses 30 W.
mistakes: Thinking insulation produces cold; it only slows heat transfer.

name: Thin lens equation
assumptions: Thin lens, paraxial rays (small angles). Real images have positive dᵢ in this sign convention.
example: An object 0.30 m from a lens with f = 0.10 m forms an image at 0.15 m.
mistakes: Mixing sign conventions; forgetting that virtual images give negative dᵢ.

name: Magnification
assumptions: Thin-lens sign convention: negative M means an inverted image.
example: dₒ = 0.30 m, dᵢ = 0.15 m: M = −0.5 (inverted, half size).
mistakes: Ignoring the sign, which tells you whether the image is inverted.

name: Snell's law of refraction
display: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂
assumptions: Angles are measured from the normal. If n₁ sin θ₁ / n₂ > 1 there is no refracted ray (total internal reflection).
example: Light from air into water at 45°: θ₂ = asin(sin 45° / 1.333) = 32°.
mistakes: Measuring angles from the surface instead of the normal.

name: Efficiency
display: η = useful energy out / energy in
assumptions: Energy is conserved: η can never exceed 1 (100 %); the rest is usually dissipated as heat.
example: A ramp needs 50 J of work to raise a load by 40 J of potential energy: η = 0.80.
mistakes: Claiming efficiencies above 100 %.

name: Boiling-point elevation
assumptions: Ideal dilute solution with a non-volatile solute. For water K_b = 0.512 K·kg/mol.
example: Seawater (b ≈ 0.6 mol/kg NaCl, i ≈ 2) boils about 0.6 K above pure water.
mistakes: Using molarity (mol/L) instead of molality (mol/kg of solvent).
